chunks: And Al-Husayn ibn Ibrahim narrated to me from Ahmad ibn Ali ibn Nuh from Abu Nasr Hibatullah ibn Muhammad ibn Ahmad, who said: Abu Abdillah Al-Husayn ibn Ahmad Al-Hamidi, the Bazzaz, known as Ghulam Abi Ali ibn Ja'far, known as Ibn Zuhama al-Nobakhti, and he was a hidden scholar, narrated to me: I heard Ruh ibn Abul Qasim ibn Ruh say: When Muhammad ibn Ali al-Shalmaghani compiled the book 'Kitab al-Taklif', the Shaykh (meaning Abu al-Qasim, may Allah be pleased with him) said: 'Bring it to me so that I may review it.' They brought it to him, and he read it from beginning to end. He said: 'There is nothing in it except that it has been narrated from the Imams, except for two or three instances, in which he lied about them. May Allah curse him.'

key_terms.الشَّيْخُ: The Shaykh, referring to a senior respected scholar
key_terms.شَيْخًا مُسْتَتِرًا: A hidden scholar (who did not publicly claim high status)
key_terms.كِتَابَ التَّكْلِيفِ: Kitab al-Taklif (The Book of Obligations), a specific theological/jurisprudential work

ai.seo_question: What did the scholar Ruh ibn Abul Qasim say about the authenticity of Muhammad ibn Ali al-Shalmaghani's book Kitab al-Taklif?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Kitab al-Ghayba* highlights the rigorous critical scrutiny applied to claimants of deputyship during the Minor and Major Gheebah periods. Ruh ibn Abi Qasim’s detailed review of al-Shalmaghani’s *Kitab al-Taklif* serves as a key example of distinguishing between authentic Imamī teachings and fabricated attributions, a crucial criterion for validating religious authority. The specific curse pronounced on the few false narrations underscores the high stakes of accuracy in preserving the Imams' teachings during times of occultation.
